extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners (Office personnel) and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance from the MPEP on how to establish and articulate a prima facie case of obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103, including required factual findings, permissible rationales (A–G), and examples illustrating predictability, teaching away, motivation to combine, and secondary considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impermissible hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge of applicant’s disclosure must be put aside in determining whether the invention 'as a whole' would have been obvious at that time to a person of ordinary skill; impermissible hindsight must be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tendency to resort to hindsight based upon applicant's disclosure is often difficult to avoid due to examination, but the legal conclusion must be reached on the basis of facts gleaned from the prior art (no reliance on applicant's disclosure to create an artificial motivation or teaching).

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish a prima facie case with clear articulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The key to supporting any rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is the clear articulation of the reason(s) why the claimed invention would have been obvious; analysis supporting a rejection should be 'made explicit'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections cannot be sustained with mere conclusory statements; there must be articulated reasoning with some rational underpinning (citing KSR, In re Kahn). The examiner must explain why a person of ordinary skill would have found the invention obvious, and link factual findings to the legal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of proof — preponderance of evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The ultimate determination of patentability is based on the entire record by a preponderance of the evidence; the examiner must provide evidence showing that the reference teachings establish a prima facie case of obviousness is more probable than not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The examiner's evidence, considered as a whole, must be more convincing than the evidence offered in opposition. Cite In re Oetiker and related MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider applicant-submitted evidence and rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: When an applicant submits evidence (in the specification or in reply), the examiner must reconsider patentability and make decisions based on all evidence, including applicant submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A decision to make or maintain a rejection in the face of all the evidence must show it was based on the totality of the evidence; facts established by rebuttal evidence must be evaluated along with the facts on which the conclusion of obviousness was reached (In re Eli Lilly; In re Piasecki; see MPEP § 706.02(j)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide an explicit, reasoned explanation (KSR/Ball Aerosol)
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel must provide a reasoned explanation as to why the invention as claimed would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'analysis that should be made explicit' refers to the court's analysis. Examiners may properly rely on inferences, creative steps, routine steps, common sense and ordinary ingenuity, but must still articulate factual findings and reasoned explanation (Ball Aerosol, KSR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve the Graham factual inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner must resolve the Graham inquiries (scope and content of the prior art; differences between prior art and claims; level of ordinary skill; and objective indicia/secondary considerations) before applying obviousness rationales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any additional factual findings based on the Graham inquiries that are necessary in view of the facts of the case must be made and explained to support a conclusion of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale A — Combining prior art elements according to known methods to yield predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: To use this rationale, examiner must find (1) prior art included each claimed element (not necessarily in a single reference); (2) one of ordinary skill could have combined the elements by known methods and each element performs the same function as separately; (3) a person of ordinary skill would have recognized that the results were predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary to explain obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rationale is that all claimed elements were known and their combination yields nothing more than predictable results (KSR). If any of these findings cannot be made, this rationale cannot support obviousness. Examples illustrate 'predictable results' requirement and situations where combining fails (Adams, Omeprazole, Crocs, Sundance). Examiners must identify a reason that would have prompted combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale B — Simple substitution of one known element for another to obtain predictable results
rubrics_metrics.description: To use this rationale, examiner must find (1) prior art device differs only by substitution of components; (2) substituted components and functions were known in the art; (3) one of ordinary skill could have substituted them and the results would have been predictable; and (4) any additional Graham-based findings necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The substitution of one known element for another yields predictable results to one of ordinary skill. If any required finding cannot be made, this rationale cannot be used. Example: In re Fout (substituting an evaporative distillation step).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale C — Use of a known technique to improve similar devices/methods/products
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to improve similar devices, methods, or products may support obviousness when factual findings show the improvement would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel must make appropriate factual findings and explain why applying the known technique to the similar device would have been predictable and within ordinary skill; additional Graham inquiries may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale D — Applying a known technique to a known device ready for improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying a known technique to a known device (method, or product) 'ready for improvement' can support obviousness when the results would have been predictable to one of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must articulate the findings showing the device was ready for improvement and that applying the technique would yield predictable results; link factual findings to the legal conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale E — 'Obvious to try' (finite predictable solutions with reasonable expectation of success)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Obvious to try' applies where choosing from a finite number of identified, predictable solutions would have provided a person of ordinary skill with a reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rationale requires evidence that the solutions were finite, predictable and that there was a reasonable expectation of success. Example: Ecolab (combining high-pressure parameter with known methods where optimization was within ordinary skill).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale F — Variations from known work in one field to another when predictable
rubrics_metrics.description: Known work in one field may prompt variations for use in the same or a different field if the variations would have been predictable to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should show why the variation would have been predictable (design incentives, market forces, or technical rationale) and include necessary Graham findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rationale G — Teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art to modify or combine
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teaching, suggestion, or motivation in the prior art that would have led one of ordinary skill to modify the prior art reference or combine teachings to arrive at the claimed invention may support obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Ball Aerosol, explicit teaching of a motivation to combine in the prior art is not always required; the court's analysis must be explicit and may rely on inferences, common sense, and ordinary ingenuity — but the examiner must articulate the chain of reasoning linking prior art to the claimed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess analogous art broadly and consider reasonable pertinence
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether references are analogous prior art (in the same field of endeavor) or reasonably pertinent to the problem addressed, construing analogous art broadly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., Wyers) emphasize broad construction of analogous art; even references from different fields may be relevant if they are reasonably pertinent to the problem being solved. Examiners should explain why a reference is analogous or pertinently relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider teachings that 'teach away' as evidence against obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art teaches away from the claimed modification or combination, this weighs against an obviousness finding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Adams, Puno/DePuy, Crocs) show that when prior art discourages the proposed change or points to disadvantages, combination may be nonobvious even if elements are present in the prior art. Examiners must identify and explain such teach-away evidence when present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require reasonable expectation of success/ability to optimize
rubrics_metrics.description: A reasonable expectation of success and the technical ability to optimize parameters (if claimed invention rests on optimization) are relevant to whether an invention would have been obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ecolab and In re O'Farrell underscore that absent the expectation of success or the ability to optimize within ordinary skill, obviousness may not be supported. Examiners should explain whether optimization was within ordinary skill and whether an expectation of success existed.
